subject: physics

moments.title: Bell Labs invents the point-contact transistor
moments.who: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, William Shockley, Bell Labs
moments.body:
On 16 December 1947, Bardeen and Brattain demonstrate amplification of an audio signal through a point-contact transistor made of germanium. Bell Labs immediately recognises the significance.

Shockley, the team's manager, had been working on a related device. He produces his own (better) bipolar junction transistor within months.
moments.takeaway: The vacuum tube has a solid-state replacement: small, cool, low-power, robust. Electronics changes forever.

moments.title: Nobel Prize and the founding of Silicon Valley
moments.body:
The trio share the Nobel Prize in Physics. Shockley moves to California and founds Shockley Semiconductor in 1956. His management style drives away his best engineers.

The 'Traitorous Eight' (Noyce, Moore, Hoerni, Last, Kleiner, Roberts, Grinich, Blank) leave to start Fairchild Semiconductor in 1957. From Fairchild come Intel (Noyce and Moore, 1968), AMD, and a long lineage of silicon companies.
moments.takeaway: Shockley's bad management arguably founded Silicon Valley, by forcing his employees to start their own companies.

moments.title: Integrated circuit
moments.body:
Kilby and Noyce independently develop the integrated circuit: multiple components on a single semiconductor substrate. Kilby's design (germanium, hand-wired) is older. Noyce's (silicon, photolithographically patterned) is the practical winner.

Integrated circuits scale: 1965 sees Gordon Moore predict transistor count per chip will double every year (later revised to every two years). 'Moore's law' holds for roughly 50 years.
moments.takeaway: Integration enables exponential scaling. A single chip eventually carries billions of transistors.

moments.title: Intel 4004 — the first microprocessor
moments.body:
Intel releases the 4004, designed for a Japanese calculator company. It contains 2,300 transistors at 10 micrometre feature size, runs at 740 kHz, and performs about 92,000 operations per second.

This 'computer on a chip' makes personal computing possible. By 1981 the IBM PC ships with an Intel 8088 (29,000 transistors). By 2024 a single Apple M-series chip contains over 130 billion transistors at 3 nanometre feature size.
moments.takeaway: A general-purpose computing device fits on a fingernail. Information technology hands the world a new infrastructure.

now.title: Semiconductors today
now.body:
Modern chips integrate over 100 billion transistors on a single die. Smartphones contain compute power that would have filled a building in 1980. Semiconductors are the foundation of communications, computing, control systems, scientific instruments, medical devices, and AI.

Fundamental physics: band theory describes electron behaviour in periodic potentials; doping creates n-type and p-type regions; junctions enable transistors, diodes, photovoltaics, LEDs.
now.open_questions: Can Moore's law continue? (Feature size is approaching atomic limits.) What replaces silicon — gallium nitride, 2D materials like graphene, carbon nanotubes? Can quantum computers (using superconducting qubits, trapped ions, photonics) outperform classical for important problems?

reflection: Shockley's later career involved increasingly racist views and a falling-out with the scientific community. His Nobel and his ideas about race are sometimes presented as separate. Should the work of a great scientist be remembered separately from their public conduct?
